claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are governed by formation of a complex multicomponent solid solution.
The multicomponent solid solution exhibits a high degree of lattice distortion.
High lattice distortion increases dislocation density.
Increased dislocation density strengthens the alloy.
Lattice distortion and dislocation density are the structural mediators governing hardness and strength.
The operative strengthening mechanisms are solid-solution strengthening and dislocation interaction.
Changing the Fe-to-Co ratio and annealing conditions will systematically alter the proposed governing behavior.
An FeCoCrNiMn alloy annealed at 600°C for 1 hour will exhibit increased hardness and strength relative to the equiatomic alloy annealed at 400°C for 30 minutes.
The predicted increase in hardness and strength is up to 20%.
The hypothesis applies from ambient temperature to 800°C.
The hypothesis applies over strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
The hypothesis applies when each constituent element is present at 20–80 at.%.
The relationship among lattice distortion, dislocation density, and strengthening may depend on composition and processing conditions.
Failure to obtain at least a 10% hardness and strength increase after annealing at 600°C for 1 hour would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: For a five-element Fe-Co-Cr-Ni-Mn alloy, requiring every element to remain at or above 20 at.% permits only the equiatomic 20 at.% composition after normalization. This precludes the proposed systematic variation of the Fe-to-Co ratio unless another element falls below 20 at.%.
